questions.stem: Prashant deposits $\text{R30000}$ into a bank account that pays a simple interest rate of $\text{7.5}$ % p.a.. How many years must he invest for to generate $\text{R45000}$ ?
solution: Substitute the values and solve for $n$: $\begin{aligned}\text{45 000}&=\text{30 000}\left(1+\text{0.075}\times n\right)\\\frac{\text{45 000}}{\text{30 000}}&=1+\text{0.075}\times n\\\frac{\text{45 000}}{\text{30 000}}-1&=\text{0.075}\times n\\\frac{\left(\frac{\text{45 000}}{\text{30 000}}\right)-1}{\text{0.075}}&=n\\n&=6\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$

sections.title: Calculations using simple and compound interest

claims.claim: Simple interest is interest calculated only on the initial amount that was invested.
The interest rate is usually labelled i.
"p.a." means per annum, that is, per year.
The interest amount is labelled I.
The opening balance in financial calculations is often called the principal, denoted P.
To use an interest rate in a calculation, write the percentage as a fraction over 100 and then as a decimal; for example 5 % = 5/100 = 0.05, and then multiply by the principal.
For a one-year investment, the interest I equals the principal P multiplied by the interest rate i, so I = P x i.
The closing balance equals the opening balance plus the interest.
For a one-year investment, the closing balance is P + I = P + P x i = P(1 + i).
The symbol n indicates the time period, which must be given in years.
The general formula for calculating simple interest is A = P(1 + in).
In A = P(1 + in), A is the accumulated amount (final).
In A = P(1 + in), the interest rate i is written as a decimal.
In A = P(1 + in), n is the number of years.

To find the accumulated amount of a deposit: write down the known values P, i (as a decimal) and n (in years), write down the formula A = P(1 + in), substitute the values, and write the final answer in words. For P = 1000, i = 0.07 and n = 3, A = 1000(1 + 0.07 x 3) = 1210.
The same method works for a loan repaid in one lump sum at the end of the term: with P = 5000, i = 0.125 and n = 2, A = 5000(1 + 0.125 x 2) = 6250, which is the amount to be paid back.
The number of years needed to invest can be found from the principal, the accumulated amount and the interest rate by rearranging the simple interest formula.

To find n: write down the known variables A, P and i, write down A = P(1 + in), substitute and solve for n by dividing both sides by P, subtracting 1 from both sides, and dividing by i, giving n = ((A/P) - 1)/i. For A = 45 000, P = 30 000 and i = 0.075, n = 6 2/3.
A fractional number of years such as n = 6 2/3 is given in the final answer as years and months: 6 years and 8 months.
To get a more accurate answer, do all the calculations on the calculator in one go, which prevents rounding-off errors from influencing the final answer.
The required interest rate can be found by rearranging the variables of the simple interest formula when the principal, the goal amount and the time are known.

To find i: write down the known variables A, P and n, write down A = P(1 + in), substitute and solve for i by dividing both sides by P, subtracting 1 from both sides, and dividing by n, giving i = ((A/P) - 1)/n. For A = 4000, P = 2500 and n = 5, i = 0.12.
A rate found as a decimal, i = 0.12, is given in the final answer as a percentage per annum: 12 % p.a.
Compound interest is the interest earned on the principal amount and on its accumulated interest.
Compound interest allows interest to be earned on interest.
With simple interest only the original investment earns interest; with compound interest the original investment and the interest earned on it both earn interest.
Compound interest is advantageous for investing money but not for taking out a loan.
With an opening balance P and an interest rate i, the closing balance at the end of the first year is P(1 + i).
The closing balance after one year is the same for compound interest as for simple interest because it only covers a single year.
The closing balance after one year becomes the opening balance for the second year of investment.
The closing balance after 2 years is [P(1 + i)] x (1 + i), which equals P(1 + i)^2.
The closing balance after 3 years is [P(1 + i)^2] x (1 + i), which equals P(1 + i)^3.
The power of the term (1 + i) is the same as the number of years.
The general formula for calculating compound interest is A = P(1 + i)^n.
In A = P(1 + i)^n, A is the accumulated amount.
In A = P(1 + i)^n, P is the principal amount.
In A = P(1 + i)^n, i is the interest written as a decimal.
In A = P(1 + i)^n, n is the number of years.
The accumulated amount at the end of the first year becomes the new principal amount for calculating the accumulated amount at the end of the second year.
For R1000 invested at 5 % p.a. compound interest, the accumulated amount at the end of the second year is A2 = 1000(1 + 0.05)^2.
For R1000 invested at 5 % p.a. compound interest, the accumulated amount at the end of the third year is A3 = 1000(1 + 0.05)^3.
To find the accumulated amount, first write down the known variables P, i and n.
Next, write down the formula A = P(1 + i)^n.
An interest rate of 6 % p.a. is entered in the formula as i = 0.06.
Substitute the values into the formula: with P = 30 000, i = 0.06 and n = 4, A = 30 000(1 + 0.06)^4 = 37 874.31.
Write the final answer as a sentence: Mpho will have R37874.31 in the account at the end of 4 years.
To find the compound interest rate, first write down the known variables A, P and n.
Substitute the known values into A = P(1 + i)^n and solve for i, giving 10 000 = 5000(1 + i)^2 in the example.
Divide both sides by the principal amount P so that (1 + i)^n is on its own: 10 000 divided by 5000 equals (1 + i)^2.
Take the square root of both sides (n = 2 in the example) to get the square root of 10 000/5000 equal to 1 + i.
Subtract 1 from both sides to isolate i: the square root of 10 000/5000, minus 1, equals i.
The value of i is given as the decimal 0.4142, to four decimal places.
The decimal i = 0.4142 is stated in the final answer as a compound interest rate of 41.42 % p.a.
Comment on the answer by comparing it with realistic returns: a typical savings account gives a return of approximately 2 % p.a. and an aggressive investment portfolio approximately 13 % p.a.
Because the required rate of 41.42 % p.a. is far above these returns, it seems unlikely that Charlie will be able to invest his money at that rate.
To compare simple and compound interest, compare the closing balances of an investment earning simple interest and an investment earning compound interest over the same period.
The closing balance for an investment earning simple interest is A = P(1 + in).
For R10 000 invested for 10 years at 9 % p.a., the closing balance with simple interest is R19 000.
For R10 000 invested for 10 years at 9 % p.a., the closing balance with compound interest, A = 10 000(1 + 0.09)^10, is R 23 673.64.
When the two investments are plotted on the same axes, their rates of change differ significantly.
Simple interest gives a straight line graph and compound interest gives an exponential graph.
The vast difference in growth is easier to see if the time period is extended to 50 years.
When earning interest on money invested, compound interest helps that amount to grow exponentially.
If money is borrowed, the accumulated amount of money owed will also increase exponentially.

As a general rule, it is not wise to buy items on credit.
Buying on credit means borrowing money to pay for the object, so you pay more for it because of the interest on the loan.
A hire purchase agreement is a financial agreement between the shop and the customer about how the customer will pay for the desired product.
The interest on a hire purchase loan is always charged at a simple interest rate and only on the amount owing.
Most hire purchase agreements require a deposit to be paid before the customer can take the product.
The principal amount of a hire purchase loan is the cash price minus the deposit.
The accumulated loan is worked out using the number of years the loan is needed for.
The total (accumulated) loan amount is divided into monthly payments over the period of the loan.
Hire purchase is charged at a simple interest rate, so always use the simple interest formula in a hire purchase question.
The monthly payment is also called the monthly instalment.
When a deposit is paid as a percentage of the cash price, first find the deposit as that percentage of the cash price (10% of R2500 = 250).
The principal P is the cash price minus the deposit (2500 - 250 = 2250), a new opening balance because the deposit is paid in cash.
The interest rate is written as a decimal in the formula (7.5 % p.a. is i = 0.075).
The number of years n is the number of months divided by 12 (24 months gives n = 24/12 = 2).
The simple interest formula used for hire purchase is A = P(1 + in).
Substitute P, i and n into A = P(1 + in) to find the accumulated loan amount (A = 2250(1 + 0.075 x 2) = 2587.50).
The monthly repayment is the accumulated loan amount divided by the number of monthly payments (2587.50 / 24 = 107.81).
If a hire purchase question does not mention a deposit, assume no deposit was paid, so the principal is the cash price.
A shop can add a monthly insurance premium to the monthly instalments of a hire purchase agreement.
The insurance premium is an amount of money paid monthly that gives the customer more time between a missed payment and possible repossession of the product.
Write down the known variables: with no deposit P is the cash price (5500), i is the rate as a decimal (0.21) and n is the months divided by 12 (54/12 = 4.5).
Use the simple interest formula to find the accumulated loan (A = 5500(1 + 0.21 x 4.5) = 10 697.50).
Divide the accumulated loan by the number of monthly payments to get the monthly instalment before insurance (10 697.50 / 54 = 198.10).
Add the monthly insurance premium to the monthly instalment to get the monthly payment (198.10 + 12.50 = 210.60).
Inflation is the average increase in the price of goods each year and is given as a percentage.
Inflation is calculated using the compound interest formula, since the rate of inflation increases year on year.
The compound interest formula used for inflation is A = P(1 + i)^n.
To find a future cost, take the current price as P, the inflation rate as a decimal i (9 % is 0.09) and the number of years as n.
Substitute into A = P(1 + i)^n to get the future price (A = 14(1 + 0.09)^4 = 19.76).
To find a past cost, take today's price as A, the inflation rate as a decimal i (11 % is 0.11) and the number of years as n; the past price is the unknown P.
Substitute the known values into A = P(1 + i)^n and solve for P (55 = P(1 + 0.11)^3).
Solve for P by dividing A by (1 + i)^n (P = 55 / (1 + 0.11)^3 = 40.22).
Family trees increase exponentially because every person born has the ability to start another family.
Population growth is calculated using the compound interest formula.
Take the current population as P, the annual growth rate as a decimal i (2.1 % is 0.021) and the number of years as n.
The expected population after n years is found with the compound interest formula A = P(1 + i)^n.
Substitute into A = P(1 + i)^n to get the expected population (A = 3 888 180(1 + 0.021)^10 = 4 786 343).
Different countries have their own currencies.
An exchange rate is written as one unit of a foreign currency equal to an amount in rands, for example euro 1 = R10.68, pound 1 = R12.41 and 1 kr = R1.37.

To find the cost in rands of an amount priced in a foreign currency, use the exchange rate in rands per unit of the foreign currency: with pound 1 = R12.41 a price of pound 4 is R49.64, and with 1 kr = R1.37 a price of 48 kr is R65.76 (the foreign amount multiplied by the rate).
To find how much foreign currency a rand amount buys, write down the equation by letting the equivalent amount in the foreign currency (euros) be x.
To buy foreign currency with rands, divide the amount of rands by the exchange rate (rands per unit of the foreign currency): x = 10 000 / 10.68 = 936.33 euros.
Write the final answer as a sentence stating the amount of foreign currency bought with the rands: Saba can buy euro 936.33 with R10000.
The three currencies most likely to be seen are the British pound (pound sign), the American dollar ($) and the euro (euro sign).
The price of oil increases when the South African rand weakens.
When the rand is weaker, the same amount of rands buys less of other currencies.
A currency gets stronger when money is invested in the country.
When we buy products imported from other countries we invest money in those countries, and as a result the rand weakens.

Prices of the same item quoted in different currencies (pound 4 in England, R20 in South Africa, 48 kr in Norway) are compared by converting the foreign prices to rands (R49.64 and R65.76), which shows the item costs more in some places than in others.
